MessageExchange.name: SupGetServiceStatus
MessageExchange.Description: Get the status of the specified Piccolo service
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
This command returns the status of the specified Service ID. It is intended to be used to determine whether there has been an exception or the command is just taking a long time to complete.
If software suspects something is wrong (e.g. after a certain period of time the response has not been received), it can issue this command. The possible outcomes are:
(1) No response - this suggests the firmware is rebooting due to an exception and software will need to retry this command later. (2) Not busy response - this suggests either the firmware rebooted due to an exception and is ready for new commands or the request was actually completed and software is mistakenly expecting more response. (3) Busy response - this suggests either the request is taking a long time to complete, software should continue to wait for the response or the service has got into an undefined state, software should either wait for the firmware to (hopefully) detect this and reboot, or software should power-cycle the device itself (wired devices only).
If the SupGetServiceStatusFlagNotSupported bit indicates a pseudo-service it means the service ID byte value is used for special purposes and does not represent an actual service. Examples are the ID bytes of "not ready" packets and I2C retry ack packets.

Revision.name: SupGetServiceStatusV1
Revision.Description: Get the status of the specified Piccolo service (version 1)

MessageExchange.name: SupResetServices
MessageExchange.Description: Reset all Piccolo services for this client
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:

Resetting the supervisor service is not required as this service does not support extended packetization and is not expected to be in a "waiting state". Resetting a service means that the services returns to "idle" state and is able to accept any new request from software.
Resetting the programming service will -
(1) exit programming mode if it was granted to "this" client. (2) close AFS file handle if it was open by AfsOpenFile. (3) stop any keep-alive messages that were being sent.
Mobile apps are expected to send this command when connecting to HA device in case the previous session was not shut down cleanly.

MessageExchange.name: DevRequestProgrammingMode
MessageExchange.Description: Request entry into or exit from programming mode
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
Requests entry to or exit from programming mode. Returns response to indicate whether request is granted. Entry or exit will be denied if another client is in programming mode (the response will be AlreadyInUse). Only the interface that entered programming mode can exit programming mode.
Force Reinit and Force Exit flags are only applicable for the Wireless interface. Firmware ignores them if a wired client enters programming mode.
On wireless disconnection, firmware exits programming mode immediately and resets all services on the wireless interface. The wireless timeout in use by the firmware can be read via the SysGetProgrammingModeTimeout command.
Exiting programming mode automatically re-enables any disabled subsystems and returns all control flags to their default states (inhibit flags off and force flags off).
The "not ready" response will never be returned in normal operation (it is a corner case that might occur in a development environment). In future, the response might return other non-zero error codes so do not rely on any value other than zero.

MessageExchange.name: DevGetEnumCapabilities
MessageExchange.Description: Get a bitmap of the capabilities supported by an enumeration definition of this firmware
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
This returns the capabilities of an enumeration definition. Each bit in the byte array determines whether a particular item is supported in the definition.
Refer to PiccoloProtocol.xml to determine the association between byte and bit position in the response and the item definition.
If the length returned is zero then either the enumeration ID doesn't exist or it doesn't support capabilities.
Note that a supported item doesn't necessarily mean it is present in a specific enumeration of the enumeration definition. Refer to the appropriate PiccoloProtocol.xml to determine whether an item is in a specific enumeration. However, use of this capabilities command to determine supported items is orthogonal to the use of multiple enumerations in PiccoloProtocol.xml. Commands that support an arbitrary set of items (such as UiExecFeature) will use this mechanism whereas commands that support specific sets of items per command revision will use the multiple enumerations mechanism and will not have a response to this command.
The presence of a enumeration item capability bit does not necessarily mean that the corresponding functionality is supported. It only means that the command that uses the enumeration will understand it as a known item. There can be many reasons why the function itself might not operate (for example; hardware configuration, current mode of the aid, business logic enforced by parameters, obsolete features, etc.)

MessageExchange.name: SysReset
MessageExchange.Description: Reset the hearing aid
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
Reboot the device through a firmware-initiated hardware reset. This causes the primary and secondary bootloaders to execute as if the device had been power cycled.
This command does return a response. Approximately 250ms after the response is returned, the firmware will disconnect from the programmer and initiate the reset process.
Software should wait at least 500ms after receiving the response to this command before attempting any new commands (to ensure that the reset process has begun).
On a wired connection, software should take the response within 250ms of it becoming available, otherwise the response will be lost. Therefore software should be polling continuously faster than every 250ms. When firmware disconnects from the wired programmer, I2C transactions will be NAK'd until the firmware has come back up. A NAK means that the device will appear to be physically disconnected from the programmer. Assuming software waits for the 500ms after receiving the response to the reset command as mentioned above, all I2C transactions will be NAK'd until the firmware is ready to enable the I2C slave interface. Software can periodically poll for this by repeatedly attempting a Piccolo command until it isn't NAK'd (at which point the expected response should be available to read). This could take up to 10 seconds. If software is not prepared to handle NAK's from the programmer then it needs to wait until it can be sure the firmware is ready. The required delay is TBD but it could be 30 seconds or more, worst case.
On a wireless connection, after the response to this command is received, software should wait for 500ms or until the Bluetooth connection is dropped and then wait for the connection to be reestablished before attempting further commands.

Revision.Description: Reset the hearing aid (version 1)

Unlike the SysReinit command, this command fully reloads the application.

See the SysReset command for the procedure to reconnect to the firmware.
The reboot flag should always be set otherwise all other arguments will be ignored and a full reset will occur.

Writes the specified device data to the device manufacturing data area in NVM (Ezairo EEPROM). Device data is specific to each device and preserved across firmware updates. Only manufacturing software and internal engineering tools are expected to use this command.
If the data is not fully provided (length is insufficient), the entry will not be modified.

During a transition phase, if the manufacturing data block being written is unpopulated, it will initialize the other values to defaults and set the version to the latest version understood by the running firmware.
For device manufacturing data that is exposed via LPI parameters in a cacheable group, software must be aware that this command could cause its cached values to become invalid.

MessageExchange.name: SysWriteMemory
MessageExchange.Description: Write bytes to memory
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
Ezairo CFX X and Y memory are addressed as 24 bit words, Ezairo CFX P memory and NFMI NVM as 32 bit words, and all other as bytes.
Length is always in bytes regardless of address space word size.
For CFX target memories, if the length is not a whole number of words, then the remaining bytes in the last word will be undefined.
For NFMI NVM target, if the length is not a whole number of words, then the remaining bytes in the last word will be preserved.
Some targets (in particular Flash) can only write successfully to areas that have been previously erased using the SysEraseMemory command.
Writing to a target not listed in the response to SysGetMemoryTargets will cause an exception.
Writing to a target that is not ready (e.g. the RF subsystem is disabled or de-configured) will be ignored.
Writing to the RIC NVM when no RIC assembly is attached will result in the RIC NVM Error status bit being set.

Revision.name: SysWriteMemoryV1
Revision.Description: Write bytes to memory (version 1)

MessageExchange.name: SysReadMemory
MessageExchange.Description: Read bytes from memory
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
Ezairo CFX X and Y memory are addressed as 24 bit words, Ezairo CFX P memory and NFMI NVM as 32 bit words, and all other as bytes.
Length is always in bytes regardless of address space word size.
Reading from a target not listed in the response to SysGetMemoryTargets will cause an exception.
Reading from a target that is not ready (e.g. the RF subsystem is disabled or de-configured) will return undefined data.
Reading from the RIC NVM when no RIC assembly is attached will result in the RIC NVM Error status bit being set and will return undefined data.

Revision.name: SysReadMemoryV1
Revision.Description: Read bytes from memory (version 1)

MessageExchange.name: SysCheckMemory
MessageExchange.Description: Generate a CRC checksum from the contents of memory
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
This command calculates the CRC checksum of a block of data in one of the memory spaces.
This is the CRC according to the CRC16-CCITT standard using the polynomial 0x1021 and an initial seed of 0xFFFF. The most significant byte is returned first.
Checking a target not listed in the response to SysGetMemoryTargets will cause an exception.
Checking a target that is not ready (e.g. the RF subsystem is disabled or de-configured) will return undefined checksum.
Checking the RIC NVM when no RIC assembly is attached will result in the RIC NVM Error status bit being set will return undefined checksum.

Revision.name: SysCheckMemoryV1
Revision.Description: Generate a CRC checksum from the contents of memory (version 1)

MessageExchange.name: SysCopyMemory
MessageExchange.Description: Copy memory from one area to another
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
This command copies data from one of the memory spaces to another (or the same). Overlapping source and target is not supported.
Copying to or from a target not listed the response to SysGetMemoryTargets will cause an exception.
Copying to target that is not ready will be ignored.
Copying from target that is not ready will cause undefined data to be copied.
Not all source and target combinations are supported, specifically only NVM (EEPRON/Flash) source and targets are supported and then BLE to BLE and NFMI to NFMI are excluded.

MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:

The meaning of each memory target ID is defined by the PpsMemoryTargetIds enumeration.
The response to this command does not depend on the current state of the subsystems. For some subsystems (e.g. RF or NFMI) memory transfer commands to these targets are only available when the subsystem is ready.

MessageExchange.name: SysEraseMemory
MessageExchange.Description: Erase memory
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
This command erases all memory in the specified range. For some target IDs the memory can only be erased by sector. This command will erase all sectors that encompass the specified byte range.
The erase value is target ID specific but guarantees that a subsequent write to the specified region will succeed.
Nothing is erased if the length is zero.
The sector size is target ID and platform specific.
Ezairo Flash and EEPROM are the only memory spaces that currently support the erase memory command. Attempting to erase a different memory space will cause an exception.

Multiple flags can be set or multiple flags can be cleared in a single command (it is not possible to set and clear flags in a single command).

Inhibiting NFMI operation prevents any NFMI incoming or outgoing traffic. It does not prevent access to NFMI memory targets and it does not prevent any of the NFMI sub-command from being accepted (however not all sub-commands are appropriate outside of normal operation).
Forcing power down should be used with care. Intended for specific test-purposes only. May cause undefined behavior if device attempts to use the NFMI subsystem. Other than the mandatory ones, none of the NFMI sub-commands are appropriate when forcing power down and none of the NFMI memory targets are appropriate for memory transfer device commands. Force power down cannot be issued if the NFMI subsystem is disabled (however it can be issued if NFMI operation is inhibited).
Forcing stay alive will prevent the WiCROS transmitter from powering down due to loss of activity detected from the WiCROS receiver. The inactivity timeout will be reset when the flag is cleared (explicitly or on exit from programming mode). This is intended to prevent the WiCROS transmitter powering itself down during an extended fitting session. MessageExchange.name: AfsReadLog
MessageExchange.Description: Read records from a log file
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
This command reads record data from the specified log file.
A zero value for the number of records to read means read all available records, otherwise it means read up to that many records. If there are fewer records available, only the actual number available will be read.
The record index determines the starting record to read and the order in which records are read. A positive index means read from oldest to newest where zero means start from the oldest record, 1 means start from the next oldest and so on. A negative index means read from newest to oldest where -1 means start from the newest record, -2 means start from the next newest and so on.
In the response, the number of records read is the actual number of records that follow in the response.
The record size and record data do not include the size of the AFS's internal CRC that it appends to records.
Records are byte packed.
The purpose of allowing multiple records to be read is to ensure a coherent set of records are returned. If records are read individually, there is a risk that the source generating the records may get in between Piccolo requests and the result will either be duplicate records or dropped records. E.g. suppose there is a daily record generated and you ask for record -1 (Monday) and record -2 (Sunday) individually. But in between, a newer record is generated (Tuesday); now -1 refers to Tuesday, -2 is Monday. The result is that you will get Monday twice.

MessageExchange.name: LpiRefreshContexts
MessageExchange.Description: Refresh all of the parameters in one or more LPI contexts
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
This command refreshes all of the parameters in all of the groups in one or more contexts.
A context count of zero means refresh all contexts.
Refreshing a context notifies the firmware that a context has been changed. Firmware will take whatever action is necessary to reapply the entire context so that the changes can take effect. Contexts can be provided in any order; they are refreshed in the order specified.
In order to reapply a context, firmware may have to reinitialize some internal functions and this may cause side effects (such as stopping and restarting audio).
Refresh does not cause control actions. For example, refreshing memory context 1 when memory 2 is the current memory does not cause the device to switch to memory 1.
Refresh does not necessarily have any effect on the current parameters in use. For example, refreshing memory context 1 when memory 2 is the current memory will have no effect.
Not all contexts have refresh support. This will be indicated in the LPI definition. Some contexts can only be refreshed with a device reset or device reinit. Refreshing such contexts has no effect.
Refresh has no effect on "auto-refresh" contexts, since, by definition, auto-refresh contexts are self-refreshing.

The CRC is calculated across all parameter values in the order given. The data bytes are considered to be formatted identically to that described for the LpiSet/GetParameters commands.
This is the CRC according to the CRC16-CCITT standard using the polynomial 0x1021 and an initial seed of 0xFFFF. The most significant byte is returned first.

MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
This command sets a cookie for use by the client to track the state of its LPI cache. The value is held independently per client. The wired connection and all the various wireless connection Piccolo GATT characteristics are considered separate clients.
The cookie is held persistently (i.e. maintained across power cycles). A client's cookie is cleared (set to zero) if any other client writes to a cacheable parameter.
The algorithm for determining the value of the cookie to set is outside the scope of this specification but it should be some unique non-zero value such as a value derived from a random number generator or a timestamp.

MessageExchange.name: LpiSetParameterById
MessageExchange.Description: Set a single LPI parameter value by ID
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
Note that unless the return code error is "Success", the value is not written.
If the datatype of the parameter is an enumerated type, then the data written is the ID of the enumerated item value (16-bit ID zero-extended to 32-bit).
If the datatype of the parameter is fixed point, then the originating floating point value should be normalized by dividing by 2^n. Where n is the negative of the number of fractional bits of the logical parameter (to the best of the caller's knowledge). If the firmware is using fewer fractional bits than the software expects then be aware that reading the value back may result in some loss of precision (the least significant fractional bits will truncated by the firmware).
If the datatype of the parameter is not fixed point then the "float_conversion" field must be zero.
The "signed" bit may only be set if the datatype is integer or fixed point.
Suppose the value that you to wish to set is -1.625 and the parameter has 1 sign bit, 3 integer and 4 fractional bits. The float should be "normalized" by dividing by the float conversion 2^n where n is -4. Then -1.625 / (2^-4) = -26 = 0xFFFFFFE6. Therefore the bytes after the context and parameter IDs are F2 FF FF FF E6.

Revision.name: LpiSetParameterByIdV1

MessageExchange.name: LpiGetParameterById
MessageExchange.Description: Get a single LPI parameter value by ID
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
If the datatype of the parameter is an enumerated type, then the data returned is the ID of the enumerated item value (16-bit ID zero-extended to 32-bit).
If the datatype of the parameter is fixed point, then the normalized return data can be converted to floating point by multiplying by 2^n. Note that n can be different to the caller's knowledge of the parameter's fractional bits.
If an error occurs, then undefined 32-bit data is returned.
Suppose the bytes returned are F2 FF FF FF E6, that means the returned value is signed, float_conversion is -4, and the normalized value is 0xFFFFFFE6 = -26. To convert back to a float, multiply by 2^n (where n is -4). So, -26 * (2^-4) = -1.625.

Revision.name: LpiGetParameterByIdV1
Revision.Description: Get a single LPI parameter value by ID (version 1)

MessageExchange.name: LpiSetParameterArrayById
MessageExchange.Description: Set a single LPI parameter's array element values by ID
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
Note that unless the return code is "success", not all values may be written.
The rules for "float_conversion" and "signed" are the same as LpiSetParameterById.
If the datatype is bool, the bits per element should be 1, if UTF-8 the bits per element should be 8, if enum the bits per element should be 16. For integer and fixed point, any width (1 to 32) is permitted (regardless of the logical parameter definition).
The number of elements that can be written is limited only by the number of elements in the parameter. If the data does not fit in a single packet, it can be sent in multiple packets ("extended packetization").

Revision.name: LpiSetParameterArrayByIdV1
Revision.Description: Set a single LPI parameter's array element values by ID (version 1)

MessageExchange.name: RtsRequestData
MessageExchange.Description: Request real time data response packets
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
This command returns repeated response structures at a rate determined by the current streaming mode that the device is in.
If an empty response is immediately received (a packet with a zero-length payload and flow control clear), then no real time data (RTD) has been started.
If RTD has been started, RTS will keep returning response packets with the flow control bit set until it is stopped. When RTD is stopped, RTS will have stopped when it returns a packet with the flow control bit clear. Note that stopping RTD is a programming service command which is asynchronous to RTS, so don't assume that the response immediately after the stop RTD command will be the final RTS response, an actual response may already be in flight.
While RTS is returning response packets over an extended period, it may also return "keep-alive" packets (zero length payload with flow control set). These can be ignored.
Currently, the only supported streaming mode for RTS is RTD. See AudStartRealTimeData.
This command is only available if the client requesting it has been granted programming mode via the programming service.

Revision.name: RtsRequestDataV1
Revision.Description: Request real time data response packets (version 1)

MessageExchange.name: DevServiceException
MessageExchange.Description: Service exception occurred
MessageExchange.EngineeringNote:
This event is generated when a service exception occurs and the client making the service request is subscribed to this event. It is only sent to the offending client.
If this event is not subscribed to by the client that originated the request that caused the exception, then the hearing aid uses its regular exception handling mechanism (reboot).
The service that caused the exception will have been reset and any pending commands and responses aborted.
If the request packet that contained the command that caused the exception had other commands preceding the offending command, those commands might have succeeded although any pending successful responses will be lost.
If the request packet that contained the command that caused the exception had other commands following the offending command, those commands will be abandoned.
If the request packet that contained the command that caused the exception required additional request packets to complete, software should abandon those additional request packets.
If this occurs, it is advisable for software to issue a SupResetServices command to get the interface back to a known state.
Exception codes match the QP exception codes used in DevGetException.

In general, files should only be saved if the source and target files have matching versions and the preservable property is true in the manifest.xml. Context data files should only be copied if the contexts definitions in PiccoloInterface.xml are identical.
